summary: This best current practice gives guidelines for authors and reviewers of specifications containing YANG modules. The recommendations and procedures aim to improve interoperability and usability of NETCONF and RESTCONF implementations. It was later replaced by RFC 9907.

plainLanguage.summary: A style guide for people who write network data forms, so the forms are neat and work together. It was later replaced by RFC 9907.

subtitle: The IETF's rulebook for writing and reviewing YANG data models so they work well in NETCONF and RESTCONF.

tldr.problem: YANG makes many useful constructs optional and allows things that servers are not required to support, so modules written by different authors can differ in quality and interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets a higher bar for IETF YANG modules: required document sections, naming and namespace conventions, usage rules for types, XPath, augments and features, and a review checklist.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 6087, was updated by RFC 8819, and has since been obsoleted by RFC 9907.

facts.label: Minimum deprecated period
facts.value: At least one year before obsolete

today: RFC 8407 is a Best Current Practice that obsoleted RFC 6087. It has been updated by RFC 8819 and obsoleted by RFC 9907, which is the document to consult for current YANG authoring guidelines.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Network configuration protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF need a modular set of data models that can be reused and extended over time. YANG defines the data structures, operations and notifications that a NETCONF or RESTCONF server supports.

YANG makes many constructs optional, such as the description statement, and permits things a compliant server need not support, such as infinite length identifiers or top-level mandatory nodes. This RFC sets usage guidelines that go beyond the minimum in the YANG specification, and says that only constructs every server must support can be used in IETF YANG modules.

It covers both YANG 1.1 and YANG 1.0 modules, applies to the NETCONF operations and content layers and to RESTCONF methods and resources, and is explicitly not a YANG tutorial. It obsoletes RFC 6087 and adds items such as tree diagram guidelines, YANG 1.1 guidance, a section on data node constraints and guidance for the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).
sections.plainLanguage: YANG is a language for describing the settings of network devices. This guide says how to write those descriptions carefully so everyone's devices can understand them.

sections.title: What a YANG Document Must Contain
sections.content:
An Internet-Draft containing a module MUST include narrative sections, definition sections, a Security Considerations section, an IANA Considerations section and a References section. The narrative must include an overview of scope and of the relationship to other YANG modules.

Each normative module is a code component, marked with <CODE BEGINS> and <CODE ENDS>, and its description must reference the IETF Trust Copyright statement. Example modules must not use those tags and must not contain normative text. Modules SHOULD use YANG 1.1 syntax, and tree diagrams SHOULD be included. Examples should show instance data, and use IPv4 and IPv6 addresses together or IPv6 only.

The Security Considerations section must follow the latest approved template. It must name writable data nodes that could be disruptive if abused, readable nodes that are sensitive or raise privacy concerns, and operations that could be harmful, and explain why. Each normative module must also be registered in the IETF XML Registry and the YANG Module Names registry, and modules should be validated with tools such as pyang using its --ietf option.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new YANG document needs the same parts, like a school report needs a title, body and sources. It must also warn which settings could cause trouble if someone misused them.

sections.title: Names, Prefixes and Namespaces
sections.content:
Published module names MUST be unique. IETF normative modules MUST begin with ietf-, example modules SHOULD begin with example-, and a published module name MUST NOT be reused, even if its RFC becomes Historic. The module name and namespace URI must not change once published.

Identifiers in published modules must be 1 to 64 characters long. They SHOULD use only lowercase letters, numbers and dashes, use complete words or well-known acronyms, and not repeat the parent name. They should not try to carry modeling semantics: calling a node config does not make it configuration data.

Namespaces for published and unpublished IETF modules SHOULD have the form urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang: followed by the module name. Example modules in drafts should use the domain example.com, for instance with a tag: URI. The organization, contact and description statements must be present, and each published version needs a revision statement with a reference naming the document that contains the module.
sections.plainLanguage: Give every module a unique, tidy name that starts with the right label, and never rename it after it is published, like never changing a street's name after maps were printed.

sections.title: Rules for Types, Data and XPath
sections.content:
The data guidance is a long list of small rules. Highlights:

  • Prefer the most appropriate built-in type, and reuse standard derived types such as those in RFC 6991. Use enumeration for a fixed set of values and identityref when the set must be extensible.
  • Order members of a union from most restrictive to least restrictive, because the first member that accepts a value wins.
  • Use boolean rather than empty in general, and add a description to each enum or bit.
  • A description must be present on data definitions such as containers, leaves, lists, groupings, notifications and rpcs. Top-level data nodes must not be mandatory.
  • when silently deletes nodes when its condition becomes false, while must causes a validation error. Use must for restrictions involving more than one node.
  • Avoid XPath functions and axes whose results depend on document order, such as position, last, preceding and following, unless the context is a user-ordered list.
  • deviation statements are not allowed in IETF modules; they are for documenting platform differences and belong in separate modules.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick the right kind of box for each piece of data, label every box clearly, and use simple checks instead of tricky ones that might give different answers on different devices.

sections.title: Changing Modules Over Time
sections.content:
Published modules must follow the YANG update rules in RFC 7950. In the IETF, an RFC counts as published work and an Internet-Draft as unpublished.

For lifecycle, a definition's status should not go straight from current to obsolete. It should stay deprecated for at least one year first. Definitions for future use, such as a placeholder leaf named reserved, should not be added.

An old client must not be forced to supply mandatory parameters that did not exist in the original module. A conditional augment may add mandatory nodes only when its condition is a when expression that the old client could never satisfy, such as a new identity defined in the same module. A condition based on if-feature is not safe for this, because clients cannot control which features a server enables.

Features should be few and coarse. Tagging individual leaves such as counters with separate features is a likely misuse, and large sets of objects may be better placed in a separate module.
sections.plainLanguage: When you update a form, people who filled in the old one must still be able to use it, so you cannot suddenly make them answer new required questions.

sections.title: Operational State and the NMDA Transition
sections.content:
Operational state used to be modeled only as config false data outside any datastore, which complicated XPath. With the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA), operational state lives in the operational state datastore, which also holds the operational values of configuration data, so there is no longer a need to duplicate structures.

New modules SHOULD be designed for NMDA and combine configuration with its operational state where possible. For modules published before NMDA, the guidance is to republish them in NMDA-compatible form and mark old state hierarchies such as /interfaces-state as deprecated, not remove them. The RFC gives the example of the interfaces model restructured in RFC 8343.

A temporary non-NMDA module can serve clients that do not understand NMDA. It is made by appending -state to the module name and namespace, appending -s to the prefix, keeping only the top-level config false nodes and marking them deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: Old devices kept settings and current readings in two separate lists. The new design keeps them side by side, and the old list stays around for a while, marked as going away.
